title: Cleopatra and Rome. Crime Scene Ephesus
summary: A mysterious tomb, an unexplained murder, a world in turmoil – in Ephesus, one of the most magnificent cities of the ancient world, Cleopatra’s sister Arsinoë was murdered under circumstances that remain unexplained. What role did the big players of the time – Cleopatra, Julius Caesar, Marc Anthony, and Augustus – play in it? Embark on your own investigation and discover the world of antiquity on the threshold of the Roman Imperial period. This exhibition by the Kunsthistorisches Museum is being held at the Neue Hofburg / Weltmuseum Wien. At the beginning of the 20th century, Austrian archaeologists discovered an octagonal tomb structure in Ephesus and a skeleton preserved inside it. To this day, it remains unclear who was buried in the so called “Octagon.” Based on this spectacular discovery, Crime Scene Ephesus combines archaeology, history, and the latest scientific knowledge to create a fascinating cultural and historical panorama. Alongside the “global players” of this era – Cleopatra, her allies (and lovers) Caesar and Marc Antony, and her adversary Augustus – it offers a glimpse into an age of turmoil, splendor, and cultural achievements that continue to fascinate to this day.

title: Bernini - Painter and Sculptor
summary: An exhibition by the Kunsthistorisches Museum in the Palais Lobkowitz The focus of the exhibition at Palais Lobkowitz is the Portrait of an Old Man, which was previously attributed to an anonymous painter. However, recent research suggests that the painter was none other than Gian Lorenzo Bernini. Known as the designer of St Peter’s Square in Rome and for his masterful sculptures, the Italian Baroque artist Bernini was one of the most outstanding artists of his time. This new discovery from the Kunsthistorisches Museum’s collection is all the more spectacular given that only a few of his once numerous portrait paintings have survived. Around ten prominent international loans invite visitors to rediscover the great artist from a surprising and hitherto little-noticed perspective. title: Prime Time – Travelling with a Roman Portable Sundial
summary: The special presentation Vitrine EXTRA, which periodically showcases different ancient objects as temporary additions to the permanent exhibition of the Kunsthistorisches Museum's Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities arrow_outward , focuses in its ninth edition on a Roman Portable Sundial. This is how we learn how portable sundials worked and just how accurately – or inaccurately! – they were able to tell the time. Nothingness. Silence. Eternity. Then – a bang. A Big Bang. An inception in space. The beginning of time. Then – movement, matter, stars, planets. Life. In time. Because nothing is without time. Time structures our lives. Since time immemorial, people have orientated themselves by the natural cycles of the sun and moon. Even in antiquity, people sought ways to make the passage of time visible and measurable. One of the oldest forms of timekeeping is the sundial. Whilst this stationary technical achievement worked everywhere, it was of very little use to the travelling Roman in a surprisingly mobile world – so something portable was needed. Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities, Hochparterre Maria-Theresien-Platz, 1010 Vienna Google Maps arrow_outward

title: Head and Shoulders
summary: Coin images are among the smallest portraits in the world. Making use of extremely confined space, they show finely detailed half-length likenesses, usually in profile. The small size of coin portraits frequently calls for highly symbolic imagery. The hairstyles, garments, and accessories that are depicted go beyond being aesthetically pleasing add-ons: they reflect the Zeitgeist and open a window into the cultures of bygone ages. More than a hundred coin portraits are on show from a cultural history perspective in the exhibition Head & Shoulders, illustrating several millennia of fashion and lifestyle. Like small time capsules, coins and medals preserve the elaborate hairstyles, magnificent beards, and intricate head coverings of each period. The exhibition travels through more than 2,400 years of fashion history with the help of over 100 coins. Coins were minted in large amounts and were in daily use. A coin portrait was therefore the image that was most frequently seen by a ruler’s subjects. Hence, the way the sovereigns styled themselves carried particular importance.
